messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Margaret is a 58-year-old widow who has been unemployed for the last three years, ever since the evening her husband David was killed in a car accident. She had been waiting for him to come home from work, and when the phone rang, it was not his voice but a stranger’s, telling her there had been a collision. She drove to the hospital in a fog, but he was already gone. What she remembers most vividly from that night is not the phone call or the drive, but the smell of the emergency room—sharp antiseptic, bleach, and something metallic underneath—a smell that still hits her without warning. When she tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events, the details slip away; she can hold onto fragments, but the full memory only arrives unbidden, triggered by something in her surroundings. The anniversary of his death, now three years past, arrives each October like a weight she cannot shake. In the weeks leading up to it, she finds herself more on edge, her sleep growing worse as she lies awake staring at the ceiling, certain she hears something outside. She has come to believe that the world is simply not safe, that disaster can strike without any sign, and that she must remain vigilant. Unexpected movement nearby—a bird taking off from a bush, a neighbor stepping out from behind a parked car—makes her flinch as if she is in immediate danger, her heart hammering before her mind can catch up. She has started repeatedly checking that all the doors and windows are locked, sometimes three or four times before she can settle into a chair. The sight of a car that has been hit by an accident, even a minor fender bender in a parking lot, brings the whole night rushing back: the phone call, the hospital, the smell. She avoids driving past the intersection where it happened, and she has stopped going to the grocery store on the main road because too many ambulances pass by. She knows this is not rational, but what frightens her most is the way the memory can ambush her without any warning at all—she can be standing in her own kitchen, washing dishes, and suddenly she is back in that emergency room, the smell filling her nose, her legs weak. The more she tries to push the memory away, the more the triggers seem to multiply. She found herself crying in the cereal aisle last month because a siren passed, and she had to leave her cart and walk home. Her daughter has stopped calling as often, frustrated by Margaret’s refusal to come to family dinners or let anyone visit. Margaret knows she is disappearing into her own house, but she is certain that if she lets her guard down, something worse will happen. What finally brought her to seek help was not the loneliness or the sleeplessness, but the morning she found herself on her hands and knees checking the lock on the back door for the sixth time, and she could not remember what she was afraid of anymore. She just knew she could not stop.
